questions.question: What does inorder traversal of a BST produce?
questions.explanation: Inorder traversal visits left-root-right. In a BST, all left subtree values are smaller and all right subtree values are larger, so inorder gives sorted order.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching in a balanced BST?
questions.explanation: In a balanced BST, we eliminate half the remaining nodes at each step by going left or right based on comparison, giving O(log n) time.

questions.question: When deleting a node with two children from a BST, what replaces it?
questions.explanation: We replace the node's value with its inorder successor (smallest in right subtree) or inorder predecessor (largest in left subtree), then delete that node.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of recursive tree traversal?
options: O(log n) for balanced, O(n) for skewed
questions.explanation: The recursion stack depth equals the tree height. For balanced trees, height is O(log n). For skewed trees (essentially a linked list), height is O(n).

questions.question: How do you validate if a binary tree is a valid BST?
options: Check if left child < root < right child for each node
Pass min/max bounds and verify each node falls within range
Do inorder traversal and check if array is sorted
Both B and C are correct approaches
questions.explanation: Option A is wrong - it only checks immediate children, not entire subtrees. Both passing bounds recursively and checking inorder output are valid approaches.

questions.question: In level-order traversal, what data structure is used?
questions.explanation: Level-order traversal uses a queue (FIFO) to process nodes level by level. Add children to back of queue, process from front.

questions.question: What information do you need to construct a unique binary tree?
questions.explanation: You need inorder plus either preorder or postorder. Inorder tells you which nodes are in left/right subtrees; pre/postorder tells you the root.

questions.question: What is the difference between LCA in a binary tree vs BST?
options: BST LCA can use the BST property for O(log n) vs O(n)
Binary tree LCA is always faster
questions.explanation: In a BST, if both nodes are smaller, go left; if both larger, go right. When they split, you've found the LCA. This is O(log n) vs O(n) for general binary tree.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of BST operations?
questions.explanation: When a BST becomes skewed (like a linked list), operations become O(n). This happens when inserting sorted data into a naive BST.

questions.question: For iterative preorder traversal, why do we push right child first?
options: Because stack is LIFO, so left will be processed first
questions.explanation: Stack is Last-In-First-Out. We want to process left child first (preorder: root-left-right), so we push right first so left gets popped first.

questions.question: What makes a BST iterator space-efficient at O(h)?
options: It does controlled inorder traversal, only storing nodes along current path
It converts the tree to an array first
questions.explanation: The iterator maintains a stack of at most h nodes (height of tree) - the leftmost path from current position. This is controlled inorder traversal.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of finding the kth smallest element in a BST?
questions.explanation: Using inorder traversal (which gives sorted order), we can stop after visiting k nodes. Time is O(k) which is O(n) in worst case but often much better.
